Making 11 October 2026

Fifteen formats, and the friends who post every day

Bobine started as a favour. My friends film all day and edit all night. I wanted to give them their evenings back without taking their footage away from them.

There is a particular tiredness in a creator at midnight, scrubbing a timeline on a phone, looking for the one second where the laugh lands. I had watched it enough times to want to fix it. So the first rule of Bobine was written before any code: the footage stays on the phone. Nothing uploads. The edit runs in the browser, on the device, and the only thing that travels is a short description.

The second rule came from the formats. A vlog is not a product launch, a podcast clip is not a paper collage. So each format got its own agent with its own brief, and the agent plans, cuts, looks at its own work and repairs what it got wrong. You give it your music and it cuts on the beats. You tell it shorter, warmer, bigger captions, and it does that.

To show it, I did the only honest thing: I cut thirteen one minute edits from real footage, each in both ratios, and put them on the landing page next to the raw clips so anyone can compare. Then I wrote the method down in a book, because the best edit is the one you filmed for. The guide came after, fifty pages with the app's own screens, in French and English.

It is French first. That was never a question. The people I built it for think in French, and the English is one tap away for everyone else.

The thirteen edits and the fifty second motion that explains all this are in the gallery here, and at bobine-tau.vercel.app.
